1.pericope_label: Blessed is he that considereth the poor... the Lord will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing

schools.summary: Fix the philology and the occasion: Ellicott canvasses poor, sick and 'sick at heart' and decides for physical sickness on the strength of v.3, granting that the verb 'implies wise as well as kindly consideration'; Delitzsch places the psalm at Absalom's persecution, pairs it with Psalm 55 over the faithless bosom-friend, and notes that two ashrey psalms close a First Book which opened with the same word.

Calvin rejects the benevolent reading outright — the blessing falls on 'the considerate candour of those who judge wisely and charitably of men in adversity', since 'the participle cannot be explained in any other way'; Gill reads the poor man as Christ himself, singular in the Hebrew, 'who became poor for our sakes', and takes the promises of preservation and strengthening spiritually.

Clarke makes the verse imitation of God's mercy, defends the occasion as David's own sickness, is severe on any messianic reading beyond v.9, and glosses the turned bed as a literal shaking-out of the sickbed.

Henry offers two applications without choosing — the blessing on David's loyal friends, or on David himself, who had 'the testimony of his conscience... that he had considered the poor' while at court; Spurgeon defines the poor as 'poor in substance, weak in bodily strength, despised in repute, and desponding in spirit', the world deserting them 'as the Amalekite left his dying servant'.

Augustine reads the psalm by his standing rule that Christ speaks now as Head and now in the person of his Body, 'but so that the words sound as from the mouth of one', preaching it on the Feast of the Martyrs as belonging to the Passion.

debates.question: What does it mean to consider the poor?

positions.view: Practical mercy to the destitute and the sick — 'God is merciful; he will have man to resemble him'.
Not almsgiving but charitable judgment of the afflicted, refusing to read suffering as a verdict.
Sympathy with the physically sick, the Hebrew word being decided by the sickbed of v.3.
The poor man is Christ, the noun being singular.
Throughout — Gill by the singular noun, Augustine by the Head-and-Body rule.
Only at v.9, and there by accommodation: 'as to any other direct reference to Christ, I believe the Psalm has none.'
Historical throughout, the psalm carrying 'the most distinctly impressed individual physiognomy of the writer'.

outliers.view: The only voice to deny that the opening beatitude is about kindness to the poor at all.

themes: Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the Lord will deliver him in time of trouble.
The Lord will preserve him, and keep him alive; and he shall be blessed upon the earth: and thou wilt not deliver him unto the will of his enemies.
The Lord will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness.

4.pericope_label: Heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee... yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, hath lifted up his heel against me

schools.summary: Read the sickroom scene as reportage: Ellicott praises the poet for looking 'into his own heart for its evil before exposing that of his friends', renders vanity as lies, and lays out the double ambiguity of 'an evil disease' — noun and verb alike — reporting the modern preference for a wound 'poured out' as in metal-casting while judging it unsuitable; Delitzsch supplies the mechanism, the visitor's intelligence being what the whisperers spread.
Gill takes the disease as no bodily malady but 'a word of Belial', a charge of blasphemy and sedition, or the cross itself, and names the betrayer as Judas outright, 'the man of my peace'.

Clarke weighs Ahithophel and rejects him for an unnamed secret enemy, presses 'the man of my peace' as the man who kissed with a greeting of peace and 'thus gave the agreed-on signal to my murderers', and leaves the prophecy question open; Wesley states the double sense as doctrine and explains the lifted heel from horsemanship.

Henry catalogues the enemies' cruelty, insulting a sick man 'designing thereby to grieve his spirit, to ruin his reputation'; Spurgeon hears 'a controversy between the pleader and his God', with the plea laid 'at the feet of mercy' rather than of justice.

debates.question: Who is the visitor of v.6?

positions.view: Absalom, on a report from 'a late learned writer'.
Not Ahithophel but some unnamed secret enemy come to see 'whether death was despatching his work'.
A single individual singled out from the body of enemies, unnamed.
Not a disease at all but 'a word of Belial' — a wicked accusation, or the shameful death of the cross.
'A thing, word, or pestilence of Belial': a diabolical malady, incurable without a miracle.
Undecidable between speech and sickness, and between 'cleave' and 'pour forth'; the metal-casting image is preferred by moderns but does not suit the context.
Directly to Judas, called and qualified by Christ himself.
Either prophecy or accommodation — he will not decide.
Both: 'literally fulfilled in David, and yet the Holy Ghost looked farther in them, even to Christ and Judas.'

outliers.view: The only voice to reach for a literary parallel to the deathbed visit, and the only one to leave 'an evil disease' formally undecided.

themes: I said, Lord, be merciful unto me: heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee.
Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish?
And if he come to see me, he speaketh vanity: his heart gathereth iniquity to itself; when he goeth abroad, he telleth it.
All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt.
An evil disease, say they, cleaveth fast unto him: and now that he lieth he shall rise up no more.
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.

10.pericope_label: But thou, O Lord, be merciful unto me, and raise me up... Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting

schools.summary: Read the close as answered prayer and formal seal: Ellicott corrects 'I know' to a future and observes at v.12 that 'here we seem to have the acknowledgment that the prayer just uttered is answered', then states that the doxology 'is no part of the psalm, but a formal close to the first book'; Delitzsch adds that 'from aeon to aeon' is, on rabbinic authority, 'directed against those who deny the truth of the future world', and that the doubled Amen 'seals it in a climactic form'.

Gill allows no literal sense to the raising — 'not from a bed of illness... but from the dead' — makes it a prayer of faith founded on promise, takes integrity as sinlessness, and leaves the doxology's speaker open between Messiah and Church.

Clarke keeps the raising literal while allowing the christological application, argues the favour from the counterfactual, and collects the ancient renderings of the Amen down to the Old Psalter's Middle English; Wesley defends the requital as magisterial duty and supplies the fivefold pattern of the Psalter's book-closings.

Spurgeon concedes the requital is 'a truly Old Testament sentence, and quite aside from the spirit of Christianity' before defending it from David's office, catches the pivot in the words 'but, thou!', and lowers the bar honestly: 'what if the believer has no triumph over his foes, he must be glad that they do not triumph over him.'

debates.question: Can 'that I may requite them' be defended?

positions.view: Only by office: it is 'quite aside from the spirit of Christianity', but David held magisterial office and sought no personal revenge.
Yes, as duty — 'which being now a magistrate, he was obliged to do'.
Recovery from sickness, with the resurrection as a secondary application.
The resurrection only — 'not from a bed of illness... but from the dead'.
Both at once: 'recover me from my sickness... Jesus was raised up from the grave; his descent was ended by an ascent.'

outliers.view: Alone in tracing the Amen through the Chaldee and the Middle English Old Psalter rather than expounding it.

themes: But thou, O Lord, be merciful unto me, and raise me up, that I may requite them.
By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me.
And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever.
Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.
